Background: Nutritional biomarkers are essential for assessing the impact of dietary interventions on health. Amino Acids (AA) serve as potential biomarkers due to their role in metabolic pathways, although the influence of combining macronutrients on AA metabolism remains unclear. Objective: This study aims to evaluate the effects of combining macronutrients (fat, protein, and fiber) on AA metabolism. Methods: A dietary intervention was conducted with 41 participants who were assigned to two groups: the Protein Fat (PF) group and the Protein Fat and Fiber (PFF) group. AA concentration was measured using LC-MS/MS. Results: Our findings indicated that combining macronutrients reduced plasma levels of AA with statistically significant differences between the two diets ( p < 0.05 for EAA and BCAA; p < 0,01 for NEAA and AAA). Metabolic profile analysis showed differences between the groups, especially at 55 days (55 D) (R2X: 0.749; R2Y: 0.589; Q2: 0.582, p < 0.001) and 98 days (98 D) (R2X: 0.886; R2Y: 0.7; Q2: 0.605, p < 0.001). Five metabolites (leucine, asparagine, alanine, cysteine, and creatine) were the most influential factors in group differentiation (VIP score), with values ranging between 1.04 and 1.75. Conclusions: The combination of macronutrients led to a significant reduction in plasma amino acids and amines in the PFF group, with recovery post-intervention. These findings highlight the possibility that these metabolites are related to different health statuses. amino acids diet mass spectrometry plasma Scientific Foundation of Caja Rural de Soria CASVE-NM-21-525 This work was supported by the Scientific Foundation of Caja Rural de Soria grant number CASVE-NM-21-525.

extracted_data.document_summary: This clinical trial investigated the impact of two distinct dietary interventions, Protein Fat (PF) and Protein Fat and Fiber (PFF), on plasma amino acid and amine profiles in a Mediterranean female cohort (cloistered nuns). The study found that combining macronutrients significantly reduced plasma levels of amino acids and amines, particularly in the PFF group, with some recovery post-intervention. Metabolic profile analysis showed significant differences between groups at 55 and 98 days, identifying leucine, asparagine, alanine, cysteine, and creatine as key differentiating metabolites, and also observed significant alterations in EAA/NEAA and Kyn/Trp ratios.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 132-day dietary intervention with 41 participants assigned to two groups: Protein Fat (PF) and Protein Fat and Fiber (PFF). The PF group consumed 150g of pork belly (standardized to approximately 20g protein and 40g fat per 100g product) with other menu items. The PFF group consumed 200g of vegetables (cardoon or borage) along with 150g pork belly (twice a week) and other daily menu items. Total menu and physical activity were identical between groups. No dose-response comparisons beyond the defined dietary groups were reported, but effects were monitored at 55, 98, and 132 days.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Plasma AA levels were significantly reduced in the PFF group throughout the intervention, with decreases observed from baseline. In the PF group, levels decreased only until day 55. Post-intervention, levels tended to recover in both diets. Statistically significant differences were found between the two diets for total AA.
